steps.title: Find the place
steps.lead: The dashed box is around Habiganj, a town in Bangladesh. Floods hit this region in July 2026.
body: First NISAR image (30 June 2026); not assumed to be dry or pre-flood. The numbered points are the inspection areas.
Grey tones are the radar signal returned from the surface: dark means low backscatter (smooth surfaces; can be open water), bright means high backscatter (vegetation, buildings).
Dark areas in this image can also be wet soil or smooth, flat fields, so this date is not labelled “dry”.
notes: Water under vegetation is not captured by this open-water approach.

steps.title: Spot the change
steps.lead: Blue means the radar signal became weaker. The biggest change is in box 1, in the top-right part.
body: The radar signal decreased in the northeast inspection area.
8.9 dB decrease — Consistent with open water; not proof of flooding.

In “Compare radar” (under “Explore the data”), the divider compares the grey images: left 30 June, right 12 July. In the northeast inspection area the mean HH went from −9.0 dB to −17.9 dB (difference −8.9 dB). This strong drop is consistent with open water appearing.
In the southwest inspection area the drop is weaker (difference −4.3 dB) and its cause is uncertain: partial water, wet soil or field work are all possible.
On 24 July the northeast area's mean was −14.1 dB. This is only a continuity observation; what happened in between is unknown.
The inspection areas were chosen where the change was strongest; they are not an unbiased sample.
notes: A drop in backscatter is consistent with open water but is not, on its own, evidence of flooding (wet soil, flooded fields, harvest).
The radar images are 3 separate observations; switching between them is not a real-time view of flood progression.

steps.title: What else do we know?
steps.lead: Two other satellites also saw signs of water in the top-right part, on nearby days. The blue patches show possible water — not confirmed flooding.
body: Experimental water candidate; not a validated flood boundary. It is derived from the change between the 30 June and 12 July NISAR observations; it is not an independent water map of either date.
Landsat and Copernicus GFM also show water signals in the northeast. The blue candidate is experimental; its accuracy is unknown.
Three sources point the same way in the northeast inspection area:
• NISAR (L-band radar): mean HH changed by −8.9 dB between 30 June and 12 July.
• Landsat (optical): share with a water signal (MNDWI > 0) was 8% on 27 June and 100% on 14 July (about 29 hours after NISAR).
• Copernicus GFM (Sentinel-1): flood share was 0% on 21 June and 85% on 10 July.
• Disagreement: in the GFM observation closest to NISAR (13 July) the flood share was only 11%; this is unresolved.

At field scale: in 162 pixels (30 m) seen clearly on both Landsat dates and not water before, 100% of the new optical water matched a radar drop, and 85% of the radar drop matched optical water. The sample is small and depends on an experimental haze screen.

Experimental NISAR water candidate (semi-transparent blue): 9.8% of the study area, geometric size 2.45 km² (1.01–5.14 km² depending on the thresholds). Candidate supported by more than one source: 0.38 km². These are not validated flood areas.
False-positive rate: unknown. GFM and Landsat are inputs to the intersection layer, so agreeing with them is not an accuracy measure.
notes: The candidate thresholds are experimental and not a validated water separation; accuracy is unknown. Across 48 threshold combinations the candidate share ranges 4.0%–20.5% and the multi-source share 1.2%–1.6%.
Places outside the intersection do not mean “not flooded”.

found: The radar signal became much weaker in box 1, between 30 June and 12 July.
Landsat (a satellite that takes normal photos) saw water there on 14 July.
GFM (a flood map from another radar satellite) marked flooding there on 10 July.
unknown: The GFM map from 13 July shows little flooding in box 1. We do not know why.
Whether the possible water is flood water or water in fields.
How often the possible-water map is wrong.
Many places we could not check, because clouds and haze hid them from Landsat.

not_this: It is not a flood boundary or a validated flood area.
Areas that could not be observed (cloud, no data, excluded) do not mean “no water”.
Moving between separate observations is not a real-time view of the flood.

sources.findings: SitRep #2 dated 23 July 2026: 1.28 million people affected in 7 districts, 59 deaths (as of 22 July). The page text does not name Habiganj/Sylhet; the attached PDF text could not be extracted.
States that Habiganj, Sylhet and Moulvibazar were also affected. A UNOSAT preliminary flood extent product dated 22 July 2026 covers Habiganj; sensor and image date are not on the page.

sources.note: Contains modified Copernicus Emergency Management Service information 2026 (reprojected and reclassified). For information only; not an early warning.

reference_maps.note: A 14-day composite, not a single snapshot; individual Sentinel-1 dates are not given. A country-scale map that cannot be read at pixel level in the 5 × 5 km study area. Not used as validation.

uncertainty: The radar images are 3 separate observations; switching between them is not a real-time view of flood progression.
A drop in backscatter is consistent with open water but is not, on its own, evidence of flooding (wet soil, flooded fields, harvest).
Water under vegetation is not captured by this open-water approach.
NISAR data are a PROVISIONAL release; no noise correction was applied.

HV noise floor: the product's noise layer is given in DN² with an unspecified normalisation. Because it could not be confirmed to be in the same unit as the measured γ⁰, no HV mask was applied. How much low HV values are affected by noise is unknown.
Areas that could not be observed (cloud, no data, excluded) do not mean “no water”.
Candidate layers are not a flood boundary or flood area; no flood depth was produced.

The candidate thresholds are experimental and not a validated water separation; accuracy is unknown. Across 48 threshold combinations the candidate share ranges 4.0%–20.5% and the multi-source share 1.2%–1.6%.
The NISAR candidate's false-positive rate is unknown: the pre-registered control protocol found no suitable control area because the independent images had too few valid observations.
Results apply only to the 5 × 5 km study area and cannot be generalised beyond it.
projection_note: Layers reprojected from EPSG:32646 (10 m) to EPSG:3857, bilinear for continuous layers and nearest neighbour for classes.
candidate_rule: EXPERIMENTAL: 5×5 pixel (50 m) linear mean; ΔHH ≤ −3.0 dB and 12 Jul HH ≤ −15.0 dB (HH thresholds fixed in advance; not a validated water separation). HV is not used in the decision: the unit of the noise layer could not be verified.
